network.overall_strategy: Valine is organized around the two immediate precursor families singled out by the literature: 2-methylpropanal for Strecker chemistry and 3-methyl-2-oxobutanoic acid for alpha-ketoacid amination. Surface discharge chemistry provides formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, and HCN; hydrothermal H2-rich mixing zones are used for speculative branched-skeleton assembly and for the experimentally demonstrated reductive amination step; concentrated surface cyanide pools supply overall Strecker and Bucherer-Bergs finishing. The 10 encoded pathways are one full Strecker branch plus a 3x3 matrix obtained by combining three explicit alpha-ketoisovalerate-source hypotheses with three valine-forming finishing chemistries; product-level shock and one-pot HCHO/NH3 routes are used only as motivation for the carbonyl-growth modules because the literature treats them as mechanistically opaque.

reactions.name: Electric-discharge oxidation of methane to formaldehyde

conditions.other: electrical discharge or intense UV over a reduced local gas phase above water

reactions.mechanism: Plasma-radical oxidation and partial dehydrogenation of methane to a C1 carbonyl pool.
reactions.reasoning: Formaldehyde is a standard discharge product from reduced C/H/O mixtures. Miller established aldehyde and HCN generation as the basis of spark amino-acid chemistry, and Ring et al. later showed that such discharge systems reach valine after downstream reactions. The main caveat is environmental: strongly reducing CH4-rich conditions are easier to justify locally or transiently than as the global Hadean atmosphere (Miller, 1957; Ring et al., 1972; Trail et al., 2011).

reactions.name: Carbonyl-pool growth from formaldehyde to acetaldehyde

conditions.other: overall-net carbonyl growth in concentrated formaldehyde-rich pools

reactions.mechanism: Net C-C coupling and reduction within a formaldehyde-derived carbonyl network to generate a C2 aldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: This step is speculative at the elementary level. Heated or irradiated HCHO-rich systems do generate higher-carbon organic precursors, but the valine literature does not isolate a clean formaldehyde-to-acetaldehyde sequence. It is included here as a compact bookkeeping node connecting experimentally observed C1-rich carbonyl chemistry to the C2 aldehyde pool needed upstream of valine (Fox & Windsor, 1970; Kebukawa et al., 2017; Kebukawa, 2022; Ishikawa et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Hydrothermal homologation of acetaldehyde and formaldehyde to isobutyraldehyde

conditions.other: cool H2-rich subseafloor mixing zone; overall-net of two aldol/dehydration/hydrogenation events

reactions.mechanism: Sequential formaldehyde addition to aldehyde-derived enolates followed by dehydration and hydrogenation to the branched C4 aldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: This is an explicitly speculative bottleneck step. The literature makes clear that isobutyraldehyde is the critical Strecker precursor for valine, but the provided valine papers do not supply a directly demonstrated prebiotic synthesis of that branched aldehyde. The H2-supported homologation logic is chemically motivated by the broader reductive carbonyl chemistry discussed in modern H2-driven prebiotic networks, but the exact conversion remains open (Miller, 1957; Ring et al., 1972; Kaur et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Electric-discharge synthesis of hydrogen cyanide

conditions.other: spark discharge in a reduced local plume or impact-generated atmosphere

reactions.mechanism: Radical dehydrogenation of methane with nitrogen transfer from ammonia to HCN.
reactions.reasoning: HCN formation is one of the core mechanistic results of classical spark-discharge chemistry. Miller showed that HCN and aldehydes feed aminonitrile chemistry, and Ring et al. identified valine in the downstream amino-acid suite. As with other Miller-type steps, the geochemical caveat is that strongly reducing NH3-rich surface gas mixtures are easier to defend locally than globally (Miller, 1957; Ring et al., 1972; Trail et al., 2011).

reactions.name: Overall Strecker-hydrolysis conversion of isobutyraldehyde to valine

conditions.other: cyanide-rich pool followed by aqueous hydrolysis over days to weeks; aminonitrile intermediate omitted from the node

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia-assisted imine formation, cyanide addition to the aminonitrile, and nitrile hydrolysis to the amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: This is the classical valine Strecker route written as its overall net stoichiometry. Miller established the discharge-to-aminonitrile-to-amino-acid logic and showed that aminonitrile hydrolysis is fast enough on week timescales; Ring et al. directly detected valine in spark products consistent with this family. The hard part is not the Strecker finish but obtaining enough isobutyraldehyde (Miller, 1957; Ring et al., 1972).

reactions.name: Carboxylative dimerization of acetaldehyde to alpha-ketoisovalerate

conditions.other: CO2-rich H2-fed porewater; mineral assistance plausible but unspecified

reactions.mechanism: Speculative carboxylative coupling of two C2 aldehydes with redox adjustment to the branched C5 alpha-ketoacid.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative. Kaur et al. (2024) make the alpha-ketoisovalerate-to-valine step experimentally strong but explicitly leave alpha-ketoisovalerate origin unresolved. This compact hydrothermal C2+C2+CO2 hypothesis is included as one possible upstream solution; no direct experiment in the provided valine literature demonstrates it, so it is flagged as a bottleneck proposal rather than an established step (Huber & Wachtershauser, 2003; Kaur et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Carboxylation of acetaldehyde to pyruvate

conditions.other: anoxic CO2-rich porewater; net carboxylation node

reactions.mechanism: Speculative aldehyde carboxylation and oxidation-state reorganization to an alpha-ketoacid.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative. Pyruvate is a chemically sensible branch point for branched-chain ketoacid chemistry, but the provided valine papers do not demonstrate acetaldehyde carboxylation to pyruvate. This node is included to expose the precursor gap, not to conceal it (Huber & Wachtershauser, 2003; Kaur et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Acetolactate-like condensation of pyruvate to alpha-ketoisovalerate

conditions.other: H2-fed subseafloor pore network; overall-net acetolactate-like step

reactions.mechanism: Speculative pyruvate dimerization/decarboxylation to a branched C5 alpha-ketoacid, compressed as an overall net step.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative. The missing nonenzymatic pyruvate-to-branched-ketoacid step is one of the main open problems identified in the supplied review. This reaction is therefore a chemically motivated acetolactate-like shortcut, not a directly demonstrated transformation from the provided valine papers (Kaur et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Surface C1/C2 carbonyl assembly of alpha-ketoisovalerate

conditions.other: hot evaporitic or geothermal pool; overall-net condensation and rearrangement node

reactions.mechanism: Formose-like growth of a C1/C2 carbonyl pool to a branched alpha-ketoacid.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative. Heated and irradiated HCHO/NH3 systems clearly climb to higher complexity, but they do not directly trace alpha-ketoisovalerate, and modern work does not securely reproduce valine as a robust free product under those conditions. This node therefore re-expresses that poorly resolved carbonyl-growth chemistry as a precursor-building route rather than as a black-box direct valine step (Fox & Windsor, 1970; Kebukawa et al., 2017; Kebukawa, 2022; Ishikawa et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Nickel-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate

conditions.other: cool serpentinization-fed mixing zone, pH about 8, NH4HCO3 present, about 72 h

reactions.mechanism: Imine or iminium formation from the alpha-ketoacid and ammonia followed by surface hydrogenation.
reactions.reasoning: Directly demonstrated. Kaur et al. (2024) converted alpha-ketoisovalerate to valine under mild aqueous H2 with Ni/SiO2-Al2O3. This is one of the best-supported valine-forming final steps in the literature, although Ni gives substantial competing 2-hydroxyisovalerate (Kaur et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Meteoritic Fe-Ni-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate

conditions.other: cool serpentinization-fed mixing zone, pH about 8, NH4HCO3 present, about 72 h

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia-derived imine formation followed by hydrogenation on a meteoritic metal surface.
reactions.reasoning: Directly demonstrated. Kaur et al. (2024) showed that ground Aletai iron meteorite catalyzes alpha-ketoisovalerate reduction to valine. This variant is more geochemically naturalistic than Pd/C, but valine competes strongly with 2-hydroxyisovalerate (Kaur et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Bucherer-Bergs-type conversion of alpha-ketoisovalerate to valine

conditions.other: pH about 8.5, cyanide plus bicarbonate plus ammonia source, about 21 d at room temperature then about 14 d heating; hydantoin and N-carbamoyl intermediates omitted from the node

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide addition to the alpha-ketoacid, hydantoin formation, N-carbamoyl hydrolysis, and net release of the added one-carbon equivalent as CO2.
reactions.reasoning: Mechanistically plausible but still valine-specific speculation. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) established Bucherer-Bergs conversion of several alpha-ketoacids to amino acids through hydantoin and N-carbamoyl intermediates, but they did not directly report alpha-ketoisovalerate-to-valine. The need for concentrated cyanide, ammonia source, and bicarbonate, plus long processing times, remains a major prebiotic caveat (Pulletikurti et al., 2022).

pathways.name: Surface-discharge Strecker route
pathways.description: Surface discharge produces formaldehyde and HCN; formaldehyde is grown to acetaldehyde, a cool H2-rich hydrothermal homologation gives isobutyraldehyde, and a surface overall Strecker conversion furnishes valine. The Strecker finish is strong, while branched aldehyde generation remains the bottleneck.

pathways.name: Direct hydrothermal acetaldehyde dimerization plus Ni finishing
pathways.description: Surface carbonyl generation feeds a speculative hydrothermal direct C2+C2+CO2 route to alpha-ketoisovalerate, followed by the experimentally demonstrated Ni-catalyzed reductive amination step.

pathways.name: Direct hydrothermal acetaldehyde dimerization plus meteoritic finishing
pathways.description: The same speculative direct hydrothermal source of alpha-ketoisovalerate as in P2 is coupled to meteoritic Fe-Ni reductive amination rather than Ni/SiO2-Al2O3.

pathways.name: Direct hydrothermal acetaldehyde dimerization plus Bucherer-Bergs finishing
pathways.description: A speculative hydrothermal direct source of alpha-ketoisovalerate is followed by HCN generation and a surface Bucherer-Bergs-type conversion to valine.

pathways.name: Pyruvate branch plus Ni finishing
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde is speculatively carboxylated to pyruvate, two pyruvates are combined in an acetolactate-like hydrothermal step to alpha-ketoisovalerate, and Ni-catalyzed reductive amination gives valine.

pathways.name: Pyruvate branch plus meteoritic finishing
pathways.description: The same speculative pyruvate-to-alpha-ketoisovalerate branch as in P5 is terminated by meteoritic Fe-Ni reductive amination.

pathways.name: Pyruvate branch plus Bucherer-Bergs finishing
pathways.description: A speculative pyruvate-based hydrothermal source of alpha-ketoisovalerate is combined with surface HCN production and Bucherer-Bergs-type finishing.

pathways.name: Surface C1/C2 carbonyl assembly plus Ni finishing
pathways.description: A formaldehyde-rich surface carbonyl pool is speculatively assembled into alpha-ketoisovalerate and then converted to valine by the experimentally supported Ni-catalyzed reductive amination step.

pathways.name: Surface C1/C2 carbonyl assembly plus meteoritic finishing
pathways.description: The same speculative surface carbonyl-assembly source of alpha-ketoisovalerate as in P8 is finished by meteoritic Fe-Ni reductive amination.

pathways.name: Surface C1/C2 carbonyl assembly plus Bucherer-Bergs finishing
pathways.description: A speculative surface formaldehyde/acetaldehyde route to alpha-ketoisovalerate is paired with HCN production and Bucherer-Bergs-type finishing in a concentrated cyanide/bicarbonate pool.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the best-aligned complete route in the network: rxn_001 and rxn_004 match Miller-type discharge chemistry and rxn_005 is a classical Strecker-hydrolysis net step. The main gap is rxn_003, a speculative hydrothermal assembly of isobutyraldehyde from acetaldehyde, formaldehyde, and H2 with no direct valine-specific literature support; rxn_002 is also a weakly anchored lumped carbonyl-growth step. Despite the pathway name, it is not purely surface chemistry, and transport of reactive aldehydes into and out of the hydrothermal setting is not justified.
suggestions: Break rxn_003 into explicit branching and reduction substeps or replace it with an experimentally supported isobutyraldehyde route
Add a physical transport and concentration mechanism linking discharge products to hydrothermal and cyanide-pool settings
Encode explicit coefficients and optionally the aminonitrile intermediate for the Strecker module

pathway_evaluations.feedback: rxn_010 is the strongest valine-forming step in the network and aligns with the mild H2/Ni reductive amination literature. The bottleneck is rxn_006: direct carboxylative dimerization of acetaldehyde to alpha-ketoisovalerate has no direct experimental support here and compresses several C-C and redox steps into one hydrothermal event. rxn_002 is also a speculative carbonyl-growth module, and the natural identity of the Ni catalyst should be specified rather than implying the supported laboratory catalyst directly.
suggestions: Replace rxn_006 with a stepwise, experimentally anchored route to alpha-ketoisovalerate
Specify a realistic natural Ni-bearing catalyst and H2-rich hydrothermal conditions
Add a transport mechanism from surface-generated aldehydes to the hydrothermal reaction zone

pathway_evaluations.feedback: rxn_011 is literature-grounded through meteoritic Fe-Ni catalyzed reductive amination, but it still depends on preformed alpha-ketoisovalerate. rxn_006 remains the major gap and has little direct support as written. Fresh meteoritic metal survival and localization in a hydrothermal zone need justification, and hydroxy-acid competition is substantial in the published experiments.
suggestions: Replace rxn_006 with explicit supported intermediates on the way to alpha-ketoisovalerate
Justify sourcing and persistence of fresh Fe-Ni meteoritic catalyst in the hydrothermal setting
Model competing 2-hydroxyisovalerate formation in rxn_011

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The upstream problem remains rxn_006. rxn_012 has only class-level support: Bucherer-Bergs chemistry from alpha-ketoacids is plausible, but the cited literature did not directly show alpha-ketoisovalerate to valine. The encoded step also omits the concentrated NH4+/HCO3-/CN- context and long room-temperature plus 80 C processing used experimentally.
suggestions: Add explicit hydantoin and N-carbamoyl intermediates plus the NH4+/HCO3-/CN- conditions for rxn_012
Provide a concentration mechanism for surface cyanide and bicarbonate pools
Replace rxn_006 with a supported route to alpha-ketoisovalerate

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is conceptually more coherent than direct acetaldehyde dimerization because pyruvate is an explicit intermediate and rxn_010 is experimentally demonstrated. But rxn_007 from acetaldehyde plus CO2 to pyruvate and rxn_008 from pyruvate to alpha-ketoisovalerate are both speculative in the valine literature; the latter echoes biochemistry but lacks a validated nonenzymatic counterpart. Surface-to-hydrothermal transfer also remains unmodeled.
suggestions: Add explicit acetolactate-like and dihydroxyisovalerate-like intermediates rather than one lumped rxn_008
Use or justify a literature-backed pyruvate source instead of the current rxn_007
Specify how surface carbonyl products or pyruvate are transferred into the H2/Ni hydrothermal zone

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The pyruvate branch makes the carbon logic clearer, but the two AKIV-forming steps remain hypothetical and the meteoritic reductive amination finish is less valine-selective than the Ni laboratory catalyst. As in P5, there is no direct literature closure from acetaldehyde to pyruvate to alpha-ketoisovalerate under the stated hydrothermal conditions. A transport model and product-competition model are both needed.
suggestions: Add explicit intermediates for the pyruvate to alpha-ketoisovalerate branch
Justify fresh meteoritic Fe-Ni availability in the hydrothermal setting
Quantify or model 2-hydroxyisovalerate competition in rxn_011

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The pyruvate branch makes the carbon logic clearer, but both AKIV-forming steps are hypothetical and the Bucherer-Bergs finish is only transferred by analogy, not directly shown for valine. rxn_012 also under-specifies the need for concentrated ammonia, bicarbonate, and cyanide and a long two-stage schedule. The route spans surface discharge, hydrothermal ketoacid formation, and surface cyanide chemistry without a transport model.
suggestions: Make the alpha-ketoisovalerate branch stepwise and experimentally anchored
Add NH4+/HCO3-/CN- conditions and hydantoin intermediates to rxn_012
Include a justified transfer and concentration mechanism between discharge, hydrothermal, and cyanide-pool settings

pathway_evaluations.feedback: rxn_010 is strong, but rxn_009 is the weakest upstream proposal in the network. The balance check implies acetaldehyde plus 3 formaldehyde to alpha-ketoisovalerate plus water, so the encoded step hides substantial chemistry and has no direct literature analogue for alpha-ketoisovalerate formation. That leaves the pathway short but chemically under-justified.
suggestions: Replace rxn_009 with explicit experimentally motivated carbonyl-building substeps
Add any needed oxidation sequence and catalysts for surface alpha-ketoisovalerate formation
Provide transport and concentration rationale for moving alpha-ketoisovalerate into the hydrothermal reductive amination setting

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This inherits the severe rxn_009 problem and adds the lower-selectivity meteoritic amination finish. The final step is literature-supported in principle, but the pathway is dominated by an unsupported surface alpha-ketoisovalerate assembly and an unstated mechanism for delivering that ketoacid to a meteoritic catalytic site.
suggestions: Substitute a demonstrated upstream route to alpha-ketoisovalerate
Justify catalyst sourcing and persistence for the meteoritic Fe-Ni finish
Make the three-formaldehyde requirement of rxn_009 explicit and chemically stepwise

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the least convincing complete pathway. rxn_009 is highly speculative, and rxn_012 is only a mechanistic extrapolation from general alpha-ketoacid Bucherer-Bergs chemistry rather than a direct alpha-ketoisovalerate-to-valine demonstration. Even if kept entirely at the surface, the route still needs a concrete concentration mechanism for formaldehyde, cyanide, ammonia, and bicarbonate.
suggestions: Replace rxn_009 with a supported upstream alpha-ketoisovalerate route
Add explicit NH4+/HCO3-/CN- conditions and hydantoin intermediates for rxn_012
Provide a quantified surface concentration scenario for formaldehyde, cyanide, ammonia, and bicarbonate

evaluation.network_feedback: Network validity is good: the graph is connected, molecule IDs are consistent, and the deterministic balance check reports 0 UNBALANCED reactions. However, several reactions need explicit coefficients in the encoding, especially rxn_001, rxn_002, rxn_003, rxn_004, rxn_006, rxn_008, and rxn_009; rxn_009 in particular requires three formaldehyde equivalents by the balance check. Literature alignment is strongest for the finishing chemistry in rxn_005 and rxn_010/rxn_011, and the strategy appropriately treats shock and one-pot HCHO/NH3 results as motivation rather than mechanistically explicit steps. The main weakness is upstream branched-skeleton construction: rxn_003 and especially rxn_006-rxn_009 are speculative lumped transformations with little direct prebiotic support for generating isobutyraldehyde or alpha-ketoisovalerate from the listed precursors. Environmental consistency is mixed because reactive carbonyls and ketoacids are moved between surface and hydrothermal settings without an explicit transport or concentration mechanism, and rxn_012 under-specifies the concentrated NH4+/HCO3-/CN- context of Bucherer-Bergs chemistry. Best current pathway is P1, but no pathway reaches the 0.8 approval threshold and the network as a whole is not approved.
